passages.happening:
‘These are the last words of David’ (verse 1): “The oracle of David son of Jesse, the oracle of the man raised on high, the one anointed by the God of Jacob, and the sweet psalmist of Israel” (verse 1). “The Spirit of the LORD spoke through me; His word was on my tongue” (verse 2).

The God of Israel, the Rock of Israel, has spoken to him about the just ruler: ‘He who rules the people with justice, who rules in the fear of God, is like the light of the morning at sunrise of a cloudless dawn, the glistening after the rain on the sprouting grass of the earth’ (verses 3-4).

“Is not my house right with God? For He has established with me an everlasting covenant, ordered and secured in every part” (verse 5). But the worthless are like thorns raked aside, which no one can gather by hand, fit only for the fire (verses 6-7).
passages.hearers:
This short poem pairs with the long song of chapter 22 at the center of the closing collection. The song gave David's praise; this gives his last testimony as king and prophet. It is not literally the last thing David says in the Bible, since he speaks again in 1 Kings 1 and 2, but it is presented as his summing up.

Oracle is a word for a prophet's utterance, almost always used of the LORD's own speech, as in the common phrase declares the LORD. Using it for David's words, and saying that the Spirit of the LORD spoke through him, presents David as a prophet as well as a king. The sweet psalmist of Israel reflects his remembered role as Israel's great singer.

The picture of the just ruler is the poem's heart. He rules with justice, in the fear of God, and his rule brings life like the sun after rain. The word for just means right relationship and fair dealing, especially toward the weak. That picture shaped Israel's hope for a coming king, and it measures every king who followed.

Chapter 7 never used the word covenant. Here David names God's promise an everlasting covenant and rests his house's future on it.
passages.later:
Peter calls David a prophet in the same way: ‘But he was a prophet and knew that God had promised him on oath that He would place one of his descendants on his throne’ (Acts 2:30). A psalm calls the promise a covenant too: ‘I have made a covenant with My chosen one, I have sworn to David My servant’ (Psalm 89:3).

The word for oracle opens Balaam's sayings as well: ‘This is the prophecy of Balaam son of Beor’ (Numbers 24:3).
passages.asks: David pictured a just ruler as sunlight after rain. Ask what your influence over others, at home or at work, would look like if it were like that. And ask whose growth your words and choices help or harm.

passages.t: The Three, and water from Bethlehem
passages.happening:
‘These are the names of David’s mighty men’ (verse 8). Josheb-basshebeth is chief of the Three. Eleazar stands his ground when Israel retreats and strikes the Philistines until his hand is weary and sticks to his sword. ‘The LORD brought about a great victory that day’ (verse 10). Shammah takes his stand in a field of lentils when the troops flee, ‘So the LORD brought about a great victory’ (verse 12).

At harvest time three of the thirty chief men come to David at the cave of Adullam, while the Philistines are camped in the Valley of Rephaim and hold Bethlehem. David longed for water and said, “Oh, that someone would get me a drink of water from the well near the gate of Bethlehem!” (verse 15).

The three mighty men break through the Philistine camp, draw water from the well, and bring it to David. ‘But he refused to drink it; instead, he poured it out to the LORD’ (verse 16), saying, “Far be it from me, O LORD, to do this! Is this not the blood of the men who risked their lives?” (verse 17).
passages.hearers:
Then the chapter turns from the king to the men around him. David did not win his kingdom alone. These stories come mostly from his wars with the Philistines, from the cave of Adullam through his early years as king. The Valley of Rephaim lay southwest of Jerusalem, and a Philistine garrison in Bethlehem, David's own town, shows how far into Judah their power reached before David broke it.

Ancient kings kept bands of elite warriors, and honor among them was ranked and remembered: the Three at the top, the Thirty a wider circle. The stories are told in a spare pattern, a name, a deed, and the note that the LORD brought about a great victory. The credit stays with God.

The water from Bethlehem shows what loyalty meant in that world. Three men risked death for a wish their leader barely said aloud. David's refusal to drink is an act of worship. In Israel blood belonged to God, and the blood of sacrifices was poured out, not consumed. Treating the water as the men's blood, David pours it out to the LORD instead of enjoying what their lives had bought.
passages.later: The law gave the reason blood belonged to God: ‘For the life of the flesh is in the blood’ (Leviticus 17:11). Chronicles tells the same scene: ‘How can I drink the blood of these men who risked their lives?’ (1 Chronicles 11:19).
passages.asks: David poured out the water because it had cost other men their safety. Ask what gifts you have received that cost others dearly. And ask how you might honor what they gave, instead of simply enjoying it.

passages.happening:
Abishai, Joab's brother, is chief of the Three and wins a name among them (verses 18-19). Benaiah son of Jehoiada, ‘a man of many exploits’ (verse 20), strikes down two champions of Moab, kills a lion in a pit on a snowy day, and kills a huge Egyptian with his own spear. David puts him over his guard (verses 20-23).

Then comes the list of the Thirty. It begins with ‘Asahel the brother of Joab’ (verse 24), and it runs through names from many places: Elhanan of Bethlehem, Ira of Tekoa, Eliam son of Ahithophel, Igal of Zobah, Zelek the Ammonite. It ends, ‘and Uriah the Hittite. There were thirty-seven in all’ (verse 39).
passages.hearers:
The list is ranked and arranged in tiers. It names men not only from Judah and Benjamin but also foreigners: an Ammonite, a man from the Aramean kingdom of Zobah, and a Hittite. Eliam son of Ahithophel may be the Eliam named as Bathsheba's father, which would make David's adviser Ahithophel her grandfather, though the text never draws that link.

The total of thirty-seven does not match a simple count of the names. Interpreters explain it in different ways, such as counting Joab and the leading heroes, or treating the Thirty as a company whose members changed over time as men died.

A parallel list of David's mighty men stands in Chronicles, with some differences in names and numbers. There the first hero is called Jashobeam, and he kills three hundred rather than eight hundred.
passages.later: Chronicles keeps the same roll of honor, and there Uriah's name is not the last: ‘Uriah the Hittite, Zabad son of Ahlai’ (1 Chronicles 11:41), and the list goes on.
passages.hard:
Why does the list of heroes end with Uriah the Hittite?

Uriah was one of David's loyal warriors, and David took his wife and arranged his death. His name at the end of the roll of honor is no accident of listing. The Chronicles version continues past him with more names, but 2 Samuel stops here.

Most interpreters see a deliberate note of judgment and grief, closing the same chapter that opened with David's claim that his house is right with God. It shows the Bible's refusal to write a triumphant royal history. The king's glory and the king's sin are set side by side, and the reader is left to feel the weight of both.
passages.asks: The list of David's heroes ends with the man he betrayed. Ask why Scripture keeps reminding the reader of David's sin even in his last chapters. And ask whose name in your own story you would rather leave off the list.
